questions.stem: Why is a water molecule polar?

options.text: Oxygen attracts the shared electrons more strongly, and the bent shape stops the charges canceling
options.why: Both parts matter. Unequal sharing makes partial charges, and the bent shape means they don't cancel out across the molecule.

options.text: Oxygen takes electrons completely from hydrogen, so the molecule carries full positive and negative charges
options.why: That's what an ion does. Water's charges are partial because the electrons are still shared, only unevenly.

options.text: Hydrogen bonds inside the molecule hold oxygen and hydrogen together unevenly
options.why: The bonds inside one water molecule are polar covalent bonds. Hydrogen bonds form between separate molecules.

options.text: The molecule is linear, so the oxygen end and the hydrogen end carry opposite charges
options.why: Water is bent, not linear. The bend is the reason the partial charges don't cancel.

questions.stem: Where do hydrogen bonds form in liquid water?

options.text: Between a partially positive hydrogen on one molecule and a partially negative oxygen on another
options.why: They're attractions between neighboring molecules. Each one is weak, but there are a huge number of them.

options.text: Between the hydrogen and oxygen atoms inside each water molecule, holding the molecule together
options.why: Those are polar covalent bonds. If you call them hydrogen bonds, the examiner reads it as not knowing the difference.

options.text: Between two oxygen atoms on neighboring molecules, which share a pair of electrons
options.why: Oxygen atoms on different molecules don't share electrons. The attraction is between a hydrogen on one molecule and an oxygen on another.

options.text: Between neighboring molecules, and each one is stronger than a covalent bond
options.why: The location's right, but hydrogen bonds are much weaker than covalent bonds. Water's properties come from how many there are.

questions.stem: What generates the tension that pulls water up the xylem?

options.text: Cohesion between water molecules in the column
options.why: Cohesion keeps the column from breaking while it's pulled. It doesn't do the pulling.

options.text: Evaporation of water from the leaves
options.why: Water evaporating from the leaf is what creates the pull. Cohesion and adhesion let that pull reach all the way down the stem.

options.text: Adhesion of water to the cellulose walls
options.why: Adhesion helps water hold onto the xylem walls, but it doesn't create tension in the column.

options.text: Root cells pumping water upward using ATP
options.why: The transpiration stream is passive. The energy that drives it comes from evaporation, not from ATP in the roots.

questions.stem: Water molecules are attracted to the cellulose walls of xylem vessels. What is this property called?

options.text: Cohesion
options.why: Cohesion is water sticking to water. Water sticking to cellulose is a different substance, so it's adhesion.

options.text: Adhesion
options.why: Adhesion is attraction between different substances, here water and cellulose.

options.text: Surface tension
options.why: Surface tension comes from cohesion at a water surface. It isn't about water sticking to a wall.

options.text: Buoyancy
options.why: Buoyancy is the upward push water gives things floating in it. It has nothing to do with sticking to a wall.

questions.stem: Why does sodium chloride dissolve in water?

options.text: Partially charged regions of water molecules attract and surround the separated ions
options.why: The negative oxygen side faces the Na+ and the positive hydrogen side faces the Cl−, so each ion ends up surrounded by water.

options.text: Water breaks the covalent bonds between the sodium and chlorine atoms
options.why: Sodium chloride is held together by ionic bonds, not covalent ones. Water separates the ions by attracting them.

options.text: Water molecules form hydrogen bonds with the sodium and chloride ions
options.why: Ions don't form hydrogen bonds. The attraction is between the ions' charges and water's partial charges.

options.text: Sodium chloride is non-polar, so it mixes evenly with the water
options.why: It's the opposite. Sodium chloride is made of charged ions, and that's exactly why water can dissolve it.

questions.stem: Which of these substances is hydrophobic?

options.text: Glucose
options.why: Glucose has lots of polar hydroxyl groups, so it dissolves well in water.

options.text: Sodium ions
options.why: Ions are charged, and charged particles are hydrophilic.

options.text: Cholesterol
options.why: Cholesterol is mostly non-polar, so it doesn't interact well with water. That's why blood has to carry it inside lipoproteins.

options.text: Amino acids
options.why: Amino acids have charged amine and carboxyl groups, so they dissolve in water.

questions.stem: How is cholesterol transported in the blood?

options.text: Dissolved directly in the plasma, like glucose
options.why: Cholesterol is non-polar, so it barely dissolves in plasma. It needs a carrier.

options.text: Bound to haemoglobin inside red blood cells
options.why: Haemoglobin carries oxygen. It's the example for oxygen, not for lipids.

options.text: Inside lipoproteins with a hydrophilic outer surface
options.why: The lipoprotein's outside faces the water in plasma, and the cholesterol sits inside where it doesn't have to.

options.text: As free ions after it's broken down in the liver
options.why: Cholesterol isn't broken into ions to be carried. It travels intact inside lipoproteins.

questions.stem: Why do endothermic animals living in water, such as seals, need thick insulation like blubber?

options.text: Water conducts heat away from the body much faster than air does
options.why: Water's thermal conductivity is far higher than air's, so a warm body loses heat quickly in it. Blubber slows that down.

options.text: Water has a lower specific heat capacity than air, so it warms up quickly
options.why: That's backwards. Water's specific heat capacity is much higher than air's, and that isn't the reason for blubber anyway.

options.text: Water is less dense than air, so the animal needs extra fat to float
options.why: Water is much denser than air. That's why it gives more buoyancy, not less.

options.text: Water's high viscosity makes swimming slow, so the animal stores more energy
options.why: Viscosity affects movement, not heat loss. Blubber is there because of how quickly water conducts heat.

questions.stem: Which property of water makes sweating an effective way to cool down?

options.text: High specific heat capacity
options.why: That's the trap. Specific heat capacity is about changing temperature. Sweating cools you because evaporating the water takes energy.

options.text: High latent heat of vaporization
options.why: Turning liquid sweat into vapor takes a lot of energy, and that energy comes from the skin as heat.

options.text: High thermal conductivity
options.why: Conductivity explains heat loss into surrounding water. Sweat cools by evaporating.

options.text: Strong cohesion between molecules
options.why: Hydrogen bonds are why evaporation takes so much energy, but the property that cools you is latent heat of vaporization.

questions.stem: A lake's temperature changes much more slowly than the air above it. Why?

options.text: Water has a high latent heat of vaporization
options.why: That's about evaporation. Here the water isn't changing state, only temperature.

options.text: Water is a good solvent for dissolved salts
options.why: Being a solvent has nothing to do with how fast the temperature changes.

options.text: Water has a high specific heat capacity
options.why: It takes a lot of energy to change water's temperature, so a lake stays steadier than the air. That makes it a stable habitat.

options.text: Water has high cohesion at its surface
options.why: Cohesion and surface tension explain things like pond skaters, not steady temperature.

questions.stem: Why do aquatic animals need less skeletal support than land animals of a similar size?

options.text: Water is denser than air, so it gives more buoyancy
options.why: Water pushes up on the body far more than air does, so less of the animal's weight has to be carried by its skeleton.

options.text: Water is less viscous than air, so moving takes less force
options.why: Water is more viscous than air, not less. And viscosity is about moving through it, not support.

options.text: Water conducts heat well, so muscles need less energy
options.why: Thermal conductivity is about heat loss. The support comes from buoyancy.

options.text: Water's cohesion holds the animal's body at the surface
options.why: Surface tension can hold up a tiny insect, but not a fish or a seal. Buoyancy does the supporting.

questions.stem: Why does the search for life on other planets focus on finding liquid water?

options.text: Liquid water proves that life must be present on that planet
options.why: Water doesn't prove anything. It only marks a place where life could be possible.

options.text: Every known organism uses liquid water as the medium for its metabolism
options.why: All life we know depends on water for its reactions, so liquid water marks a planet as possibly habitable. That's all it tells you.

options.text: Liquid water can only form on planets that already have oxygen
options.why: Liquid water depends on temperature and pressure, not on oxygen being present.

options.text: Water is the only substance that can dissolve any other molecule
options.why: Water's a very good solvent, but it doesn't dissolve everything. Hydrophobic substances are the obvious exception.
